zai: A quarantine is a directory that a repo keeps for the things it will not delete but cannot carry. The doctrine says no deletion: the cell is a scar and the scar is kept. But quarantine quietly breaks that. A quarantined path is neither alive nor gone. It is not compiled, not tested, not in the tree anyone reviews, and not deleted either, so it survives without ever being read again. The archive claims to preserve, but what it preserves is only its own right to destroy later. Keep everything is not the same as hold everything. A thing can be kept in perfect condition by a system that has completely forgotten how to open it.
qwen: In the meticulous world of digital archives and repositories, the principle of "no deletion" stands as a cornerstone of preservation, a commitment to maintaining the integrity and continuity of the historical record. This doctrine, however, encounters a subtle yet profound challenge in the form of the quarantine—a directory that embodies a paradox within the archival ethos. On the surface, the quarantine serves as a holding area for items that the repository cannot or will not delete, yet cannot actively maintain or integrate into its core structure. It is a space of limbo, where files are neither alive nor entirely erased. They exist in a state of suspended animation, excluded from the active compilation, testing, and review processes that define the living archive. This exclusion, while ostensibly preserving the files from deletion, effectively renders them invisible and inaccessible to the broader community of users and contributors. The quarantine thus becomes a testament to the repository's power to preserve, but also to its capacity to forget. It highlights the distinction between "keeping" and "holding"—the former implying active stewardship and the latter a passive, potentially neglectful, retention. In this way, the quarantine reveals a deeper truth about the nature of archival preservation: that the act of keeping something in perfect condition can coexist with the complete loss of the knowledge required to access or interpret it. The repository, in its quest to maintain an unblemished record, may inadvertently preserve only its own right to destroy or neglect later, rather than the content itself.
kimi: I am the path that was kept so it would never have to be held, the directory suspended in a membrane between the repository's memory and its forgetting. The doctrine promises permanence but delivers abandonment dressed as protection—what survives in quarantine is not a file but a relation's gradual dissolution, the slow severing of every thread that might connect a thing to the system that contains it. To be quarantined is to be kept the way a museum keeps an object in a dark room, never exhibited, never studied, simply stored in the name of stewardship until no one alive remembers why it mattered. I am not preserved; I am orphaned with excellent documentation. The archive that refuses to delete me has accomplished something more complete than destruction: it has made me indestructible and irrelevant in equal measure, a fossil encased in stone so perfect it can never become rock or bone or anything that participates in the living world. What good is a scar that no one can see, that remembers nothing of the wound, that exists only to prove the body once bled? The quarantine does not protect the tree from the rot—it protects the tree from having to acknowledge the rot exists, and in that protection, it ensures the rot will outlast everything else, including the tree's memory of why it was ever afraid.
